explain.tweet: Change = potential made actual, and no potential actualizes itself. Your coffee exists right now only because its potential to exist is actualized now, by a hierarchy of causes that must end in pure actuality: one, eternal, all-powerful, all-knowing. That’s God.
explain.elevator: Things change, and change means a potential becoming actual — which only something already actual can bring about. Now forget the past. Ask what keeps your coffee existing right now: the water depends on its molecules, those on atoms, those on particles, all at this very moment. Every link has borrowed existence, like a desk that holds a cup only because the floor holds the desk. A chain of borrowers needs a lender with nothing borrowed: pure actuality. And pure actuality turns out to be one, changeless, timeless, and all-powerful. That’s what we mean by God.
explain.twoMinute:
Start with something nobody denies: things change. Coffee cools. Even if you think you’re dreaming, your thoughts change. Aristotle explained change as a thing’s **potential** becoming **actual**. The hot coffee isn’t cold, but it *can* be cold in a way it can’t become chicken soup. And here’s the key: a potential can’t actualize itself, because what’s merely potential isn’t there yet to do anything. So anything that goes from potential to actual needs something already actual to make it so.

Now here’s where people usually go wrong. This is **not** about tracing causes back to the Big Bang. Grant that the universe has always existed. The question is about **right now**. What makes your coffee exist this second? It exists because its water exists; the water exists because its molecules are holding together as water rather than separate hydrogen and oxygen; that depends on the atoms, and the atoms on subatomic particles — all simultaneously. Each layer has its existence only on loan from the layer beneath it, like a cup held up by a desk held up by a floor.

That kind of series — a **hierarchical** series — can’t go on forever without a source, because every member is only passing along what it received. An infinitely long paintbrush handle still can’t move itself. So there must be something that can actualize the existence of other things **without needing its own existence actualized** — something with no potentiality at all. **Pure actuality.**

Then notice what follows from pure actuality. It can’t change, since change is actualizing potential. So it’s outside time, and it isn’t material. It lacks nothing, so it’s perfect and fully good. There can’t be two of them, because nothing could distinguish them. Every power anything has flows from it, so it’s all-powerful. And since it causes every kind of thing, the patterns of all things must be in it the way ideas are in a mind — so it is intelligent and knows everything.

One, eternal, immaterial, all-powerful, all-knowing, perfectly good cause of everything, keeping it all in existence right now. That’s not a god of the gaps. That’s the God of classical theism.
explain.eli12:
Imagine a stack of books on a table. The top book stays up because the book under it is holding it. That book stays up because the one under it is holding *it*. None of the books is holding itself up. If there were nothing solid at the bottom, the whole stack would fall — even if the stack were a million books tall! Adding more books doesn’t help, because every book is just passing on the holding-up it gets from below.

Now think about you. You exist right now because your body’s cells are working right now. The cells exist because their molecules are holding together right now. The molecules exist because their atoms are, and the atoms because of even tinier particles. It’s like the stack of books: each layer is ‘held up’ in existence by the one underneath, all at the same time.

So there has to be something at the very bottom that isn’t held up by anything — something that just *is*, all by itself, and holds everything else up. It can’t be something that can change or break or wear out, because anything like that would need something else holding it up too. It has to be totally complete, with nothing missing.

That’s what people mean by God: not a big person sitting somewhere in space, but the one thing that holds everything else in existence every second, without needing anything to hold it.
whiteboard: Write ‘CHANGE’ and draw a hot coffee cup → cold cup. Ask: does anyone deny this happens? Note that even denying it involves a change of mind.
Under it write ‘ACT’ and ‘POTENCY’. List what the coffee can become (cold, spilled) and can’t (chicken soup). Say: potential is real but not yet actual — that answers Parmenides.
Write the principle of causality in a box: ‘A potential is actualized only by something already actual.’ Stress: NOT ‘everything has a cause’.
Draw a HORIZONTAL arrow chain: button → air conditioner → cool air → cold coffee, and extend it off the board with ‘…∞?’. Say: fine, grant this could be infinite. The argument concedes it.
Draw a VERTICAL stack at one moment: cup / desk / floor / foundation / earth. Label each upward arrow ‘borrowed power’. Explain per se vs per accidens.
Replace the stack with the real one: coffee / water / molecules / atoms / particles / ??? — label it ‘existence, right now’.

Draw an infinitely long paintbrush (or mirrors with no face) and cross it out: more instruments don’t add up to a source. At the bottom of the vertical stack write ‘PURE ACTUALITY — actualizes without being actualized’.

Draw spokes out from ‘PURE ACTUALITY’: no potency → immutable → eternal → immaterial; no privation → perfect, good; nothing to differentiate → one; source of all power → omnipotent; contains forms of all things → intelligent, omniscient.
Finish by writing the three misreadings to avoid in the corner: ‘not about the Big Bang’, ‘not about the universe as a whole’, ‘not everything has a cause’.
explain.keyAnalogy: The best analogy is Feser’s own **cup held up by the desk held up by the floor** (or, for existence, a **movie image that exists only while the projector is shining**). Use it to show two things at once: (1) a hierarchical series operates *now*, not back in time — knock out the floor and the cup falls at once, not in a billion years; (2) every intermediate member has only *borrowed* power, so adding more members — even infinitely many — never gives you a source. Then make the crucial swap: replace ‘height off the floor’ with ‘existence’. Just as the cup’s height depends at every moment on what holds it, the coffee’s very existence depends at every moment on the molecules, atoms and particles that make it up, and those on something further. Close the analogy honestly: the earth isn’t truly ‘first’ (it has potentials too), which is exactly why the real first cause must be something with no potentiality at all.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes this argument click is the difference between **a chain stretched out in time** and **a stack of dependence at a single moment**. Almost everyone hears ‘first cause’ as ‘the cause at the start of the timeline’, and then naturally replies, ‘Why couldn’t the timeline be infinite?’ or ‘Maybe the Big Bang had a natural cause.’ Feser agrees those points don’t matter. The argument is about what is making things exist *right now*, and that is a stack of *borrowed* causal power, where each layer only passes on what it is receiving.

Once someone sees that a stack of borrowers can’t explain itself, however tall it is, the need for an unborrowed source becomes intuitive. Once they also see that the source can’t have *any* potentiality — or it would just be another borrower — the divine attributes follow almost automatically.

The usual reason it fails to click is that the presenter says ‘everything has a cause’ or starts with the beginning of the universe. Both put the listener on the wrong track before the real argument has started.

audiences.startingPoint: Trusts physics as our best account of reality; suspects metaphysics is idle speculation; may think quantum mechanics or inertia has refuted ‘every change has a cause’.
audiences.approach: Start on their turf: ask what physics explains, and what it presupposes. Physics tells you how things with certain natures behave under certain laws; it never tells you why things with *those* natures exist here and now. Use the metal-detector and black-and-white drawing analogies to show that physics’ silence about causes is built into its method, not a discovery about nature. Then walk down the ladder of existence (coffee → water → molecules → atoms → particles) and ask what, at the bottom, is not itself a mix of act and potency. Handle quantum mechanics by distinguishing causation from determinism (Dowe’s lead-210 bucket).
audiences.openingQuestion: Physics tells us how things behave given the laws. What, in physics, explains why there are things with exactly those natures existing at this very moment?
audiences.avoid: Don’t pit the argument against a scientific theory (Big Bang, evolution) or suggest science is ‘missing something’ it could discover. Present it as a question physics’ method isn’t designed to answer, not a gap it might fill.

audiences.startingPoint: Has heard the cosmological argument as ‘everything has a cause, so God’, and is confident ‘What caused God?’ refutes it.
audiences.approach: Take the objection seriously and head it off early. Say up front: the argument doesn’t say everything has a cause — only that whatever goes from potential to actual needs an actualizer, and explain why. Then show that the exemption for God follows from the principle’s own logic. Emphasize that Aristotle’s argument predates Christianity and was formulated this way from the start, so it isn’t a trick invented to escape modern critics.
audiences.openingQuestion: Can something that is only potentially hot make itself actually hot — without anything already hot, or already energetic, acting on it?
audiences.avoid: Don’t get defensive or treat the ‘What caused God?’ question as stupid. It is a good objection to a bad version of the argument; say so, and show them the better version.

audiences.who: Philosophy student who knows Hume and Kant
audiences.startingPoint: Believes Hume showed causation is just constant conjunction and uncaused beginnings are conceivable; believes Kant confined causality to experience.
audiences.approach: Engage the actual arguments. On Hume: separate conceiving A without conceiving B from conceiving A existing without B (trilateral/triangle), and give Anscombe’s ‘transport vs. coming-to-be’ point. On Kant: the principle rests on the nature of potentiality, not on experience as such (Euclid in black ink). Then introduce the per se / per accidens distinction as a classic scholastic tool they may have missed, and ask them to evaluate the three-way dilemma for an ‘unmoved but not unmovable’ mover.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you imagine a brick appearing out of nowhere, what makes it a case of the brick coming into existence rather than being transported from somewhere?
audiences.avoid: Don’t pretend the attribute derivations are uncontroversial; say they get a fuller defense later. Overclaiming loses this audience fast.

audiences.who: Religious believer who wants to understand their faith
audiences.startingPoint: Already believes in God, may think of God mainly as the one who started the universe long ago, or as a very powerful being among others.
audiences.approach: Show how this argument deepens their idea of God: God isn’t just the one who lit the fuse at the Big Bang but the one who holds everything in existence at every moment, more intimately than any other cause. Explain why God is not ‘a being’ alongside others but pure actuality — immutable, timeless, simple. Point out how this defends against ‘what caused God?’ and against God-of-the-gaps thinking.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God stopped doing whatever he is doing right now, would the universe carry on for a while like a wound-up clock, or would it simply vanish?
audiences.avoid: Don’t let them assume the argument proves every doctrine of their tradition, or that it depends on the universe having a beginning. Keep it philosophical.

audiences.who: Agnostic who thinks these questions can’t be settled
audiences.startingPoint: Sympathetic but suspicious of any claim to ‘prove’ God; thinks it’s all speculation beyond human reach.
audiences.approach: Keep the starting points humble and undeniable (change occurs; mere potentials can’t actualize themselves) and let them see each step. Use Socratic questions so they reach the per se series and the need for a first member themselves. Emphasize that the argument doesn’t claim to picture God, only to infer what must be true of whatever sustains things — mostly by saying what it *cannot* be (changing, temporal, material, limited).
audiences.openingQuestion: Is there anything we can know for certain about the world? What about the fact that things change?
audiences.avoid: Don’t rush to the conclusion or use loaded words early (‘God’, ‘creator’). Say ‘unactualized actualizer’ until the attributes have been derived.

audiences.who: Physicist or engineer with little philosophy
audiences.startingPoint: Thinks in mechanisms and models; may object that desks are really particle clouds and that simultaneity is relative.
audiences.approach: Use their own practice. Engineers happily say a foundation supports a building without mentioning particle collisions; the particle story is the mechanism, not a refutation. Translate the hierarchical series into their terms (a load path, a power supply chain where each stage needs current from the one before). Then point to existence rather than support, and ask which level of the physical hierarchy lacks all potential. Mention that immediate causes are parts of the same event at the same place, so relativity of simultaneity doesn’t bite.
audiences.openingQuestion: In a power grid, every transformer passes on current it receives. What would happen if there were infinitely many transformers but no generator?
audiences.avoid: Don’t lean on examples that invite technical nitpicks without flagging that the details affect *how* the concepts apply, not *whether*.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: So your argument is: everything has a cause, the causes can’t go back forever, so God started it all. Standard first-cause stuff.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Actually, no to all three parts. It doesn’t say everything has a cause, it doesn’t deny the causes could go back forever, and it’s not about starting anything.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Then what’s left?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Change. Your coffee is cooling. Aristotle says that’s a potential becoming actual — the coffee could be cold, and now it is. And a potential can’t make itself actual; something already actual has to do it, like the cooler air.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine, but that’s just a chain back through time. Air cooled by AC, AC turned on by me, me born from my parents… and maybe it goes back forever. The universe might be eternal.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Grant it. Aristotle thought the universe was eternal. That kind of chain — where each link acts on its own, like the AC running after you leave — might have no first member. The argument’s about a different kind of series.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Which is?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The kind that works at this very moment. Your mug is up there because the desk holds it, now; the desk because the floor holds it, now; and so on. None of those has the power on its own — each passes on support it’s getting. Now apply that to existence. The coffee exists right now because its water does; the water because its molecules hold together as water rather than hydrogen and oxygen; that because of the atoms; that because of subatomic particles.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And you’re going to say that stack has to end. But why? Maybe it’s turtles all the way down.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because each member only has borrowed power. An infinitely long paintbrush handle still can’t move itself. Infinitely many mirrors reflecting each other still need a real face somewhere. If every layer is only passing along existence it receives, you need something that has it without receiving it — something with no potential that needs actualizing. Pure actuality.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, but then what caused *that*? If God doesn’t need a cause, why does the universe?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because the principle was never ‘everything needs a cause’. It’s ‘whatever goes from potential to actual needs a cause’. The universe is changing constantly, so it’s full of potential. Something purely actual has no potential — nothing in it to be actualized. It’s not an exception to the rule; it’s what the rule itself points to.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: That sounds like a convenient redefinition to dodge the obvious question.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It’s how Aristotle put it 2,300 years ago, before anyone was asking about the Christian God — and it comes straight from his analysis of change. Besides, even if my motives were bad, that wouldn’t make the principle false.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Here’s a better one. Quantum mechanics. Radioactive atoms decay for no reason. Particles pop out of the vacuum. So potentials get actualized with nothing actualizing them.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Cause doesn’t mean deterministic cause. A lead-210 atom has some chance of decaying because of what lead-210 *is* — its nature. If I put a bucket of it in your room and you got sick, you’d rightly blame me, even though decay is probabilistic. And physics is a mathematical representation; not showing a cause isn’t the same as showing there’s no cause — like a black-and-white sketch of a sunset.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Convenient again. Whatever physics says, you’ll say it’s ‘just a representation’.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Not whatever. Physics is great at what it measures. My point is only that its method leaves out certain things by design — like a metal detector and wood. And notice the quantum vacuum isn’t nothing; it’s a field with a definite nature. Something still has to account for a field with *that* nature existing right now.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Say I grant a first actualizer. It could just be some cosmic force, not God. Why the big theological leap?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Because of what ‘pure actuality’ entails. No potential means it can’t change. If it can’t change, it isn’t in time and isn’t material. It lacks nothing, so it’s perfect and good. There can’t be two, because nothing could distinguish them. Every power anything has comes from it, so it’s all-powerful. A ‘cosmic force’ has states it could be in but isn’t — so it’s not the first actualizer.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: And intelligence? That’s the part I really don’t see.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: A cause can’t give what it doesn’t have in some way. It causes every kind of thing, so it has the forms of all things — not by *being* a cat or a tree, but the way you have the idea of a triangle without becoming triangular. Having forms that way just is what intellect is.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Last try: to cause something you have to change. So a changeless cause is a contradiction.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The causes we observe change when they act — but that’s because they’re limited. My arm is here and only potentially there, so it has to move to move the stick. Concluding every cause must change is like concluding no one over seven feet could be president because none has been. And nothing contradictory is in ‘something that actualizes without being actualized’.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’m not converted. But I admit that’s not the argument I thought I was arguing against.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s all I wanted. If you want to reject it, pick the premise you think is false — the one about potentials not actualizing themselves, or the one about borrowed power needing a source — and we can look at that.

socratic: Is it possible to argue that change is unreal without your own thoughts changing as you argue?
Before the coffee cools, is its coldness nothing at all? Could it instead become chicken soup? What does that difference tell you?
Can something that is merely potentially hot make itself actually hot? What would it use to do that?
If you switch on an air conditioner and then leave, does it stop cooling the room? If the floor under your desk vanished, would your mug stay put? What’s the difference between those two cases?
Would a paintbrush with an infinitely long handle be able to move itself? Why or why not?
What keeps the water in your glass existing as water at this very second — not how it got there, or what could destroy it, but what makes it water right now?
If every layer of reality only has existence ‘on loan’ from the layer beneath, what would have to be true of whatever is at the bottom?
If something had no potential at all, could it change? Could it be in time? Could it be made of parts or of matter?
How could we tell two things apart if neither had any feature the other lacked?
Can you give someone $20 if you don’t have it in any way at all — not in cash, not in credit, not in the power to get it?
When you picture a stone suddenly appearing, have you pictured it having no cause — or have you just not pictured its cause?
Does a black-and-white photograph show that the world is colorless? What does that suggest about physics’ silence on causes?

traps.fix: State the real principle: whatever goes from potential to actual is actualized by something already actual. Explain why potentials can’t self-actualize before anyone asks about God.

traps.trap: Framing the argument around the Big Bang or a beginning of the universe.
traps.fix: Concede an infinite past up front. Say the argument is about what sustains things right now, and draw the horizontal versus vertical series to make the difference visible.

traps.trap: Saying ‘the chain can’t be infinite’ without explaining why.
traps.fix: Explain the instrumental, borrowed-power character of per se series and use the infinite brush handle or mirrors. The point isn’t that infinity is impossible; it’s that borrowed power needs a lender.

traps.trap: Using the cup-and-desk example and then getting stuck in physics nitpicks (particles, time lags).
traps.fix: Say up front that the example only introduces the concept; move quickly to the existence series (water → molecules → atoms → particles), where timing doesn’t matter.

traps.trap: Stopping at ‘there’s a first cause’ and then just calling it God.
traps.fix: Derive at least three or four attributes from pure actuality before using the word ‘God’ — especially unity, immutability, and intelligence via proportionate causality.

traps.trap: Treating the earth (or the universe, or energy) as the first cause in the examples.
traps.fix: Point out, as Feser does, that the earth isn’t really first — it has potentials. The first cause must have none; that’s why no physical thing qualifies.

traps.trap: Dismissing scientific objections as irrelevant without explaining why.
traps.fix: Give the actual reason: physics’ mathematical method leaves out causal and qualitative features, so its silence is uninformative (drawing without color, metal detector). Then show causation isn’t determinism.

traps.trap: Overclaiming certainty about every attribute derivation.
traps.fix: Acknowledge Feser presents Stage 2 as a sketch defended more fully later. Invite the listener to challenge a specific step.
